from.content:
## Recommended fix

Catch the message at the one spot inside Orca where every file load produces it. Then it does not matter how the file was opened.

1. **One catch point in Orca.** Inside Orca, every 3MF message already goes through a single function. We add a small hook there. When JusPrin has registered a handler, the message goes to JusPrin instead of becoming a popup. The hook carries the facts: which program made the file, its version, and whether its settings were used. Plain OrcaSlicer, with no handler, behaves exactly as before. That is about 8 lines in Orca's code.
2. **JusPrin decides what to do with each message.** It never shows a popup. It writes its own plain wording, such as "This file was made in PrusaSlicer. We kept the models and used your current printer, filament and process settings."
3. **The message becomes a note on the project.** The note sits in Project details, where the product plan already puts "important profile notes". It also appears in the Send check before printing, when it actually matters. The Agent reads the same note. So after a manual open, the Agent knows the same thing it would have known if it had opened the file itself.

We considered a cheaper version that needs no Orca change: a JusPrin rule that clicks away any popup titled "Load 3MF". We rejected it for two reasons. It would also silently click away any future Orca popup with that title, even one that asks a real question. And a title can't tell a PrusaSlicer file from an old Orca file, so JusPrin could not write an accurate note.

The same hook should also carry two safety warnings that appear when a project loads: "Modified G-code" and "Customized Preset". They say the file contains custom machine code. They are common: they fire on other people's projects, and even on JusPrin's own files that use custom presets. Today the Agent clicks them away without telling anyone. Under the fix they become a *safety* note that the Agent must mention and the Send check must show.

content.text: Now the other popups, grouped into five kinds with a strategy for each.

from.content:
## Other popups users run into

We looked at every popup Orca can show during normal use: opening and saving, changing settings, slicing, printing, and starting or quitting the app. They fall into five kinds. Each kind gets one strategy, and it should be the same whether the user or the Agent started the action.

| Kind | Common examples | Strategy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. **Information only** (nothing to decide) | The 3MF messages above; "Modified G-code"; "some values were not recognized" | No popup. A note on the project that the user and the Agent both read. Safety warnings are shown before printing |
| 2. **Questions while loading a file** | "Open as a project or import models only?"; "Object looks too small, convert from inches?"; "Load these files as one object?" (when dropping several STLs); STEP import quality | Ask the user in JusPrin's own style, with the same defaults whether they opened the file or the Agent did. Today a manual open gets an Orca dialog, and the Agent gets an approval card |
| 3. **Decisions with consequences** | "Save changes before continuing?"; "Keep or discard your edited settings?"; "Restore your last session?" after a crash; stop a print; the Send dialogs | Keep them as real decisions, but present them in JusPrin's UI |
| 4. **Errors** | Loading failed; slicing failed; upload to printer failed | Show them where the user can do something about them, not in a separate box |
| 5. **Background prompts** | "New version available"; download the Bambu network plug-in; sign-in expired | Move them to Preferences and quiet notifications, as the product plan already says |

Some of Orca's messages are drawn as small banners inside the 3D view rather than as popups, for example slicing errors and upload results. These can't be seen while the user is on Home or the printer page. They need their own pass later.

content.text: Next, the bugs and gaps found along the way.

from.content:
## Problems found along the way

The first is the most serious. "Checked" means we read the code ourselves. "Survey" means an automated code search reported it and nobody has checked it yet.

| Problem | Why it matters | Checked? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JusPrin asks OrcaSlicer's update server for new versions on every launch | Whenever OrcaSlicer ships a release, JusPrin users see "New version of JusPrin" with a link to download OrcaSlicer | Checked |
| Choosing a printer model Orca can't match shows an empty popup, then crashes | App crash | Checked |
| When the Agent opens a project, Orca's "adjust these settings?" questions are answered No | Example: a vase-mode project can have vase mode turned off. A manual open would have asked the user | Survey |
| Asking the Agent to change a printer can be blocked by an Orca popup nobody answers | Happens when only the process changes while filament settings have unsaved edits, and when adding a printer | Survey |
| If the user once ticked "remember my choice: save", an Agent open that should discard changes saves instead | Can open a Save dialog in the middle of an Agent action | Survey |
| Orca's custom-machine-code check skips the last filament and the printer | The safety warning can miss unsafe code | Survey |
| On two-nozzle Bambu printers (H2D), the filament-grouping and "sync now?" prompts never appear in JusPrin | Those users silently lose a setup step | Survey |
| BambuStudio version numbers are shown wrongly, e.g. "2.6.51" | Confusing numbers in version messages | Survey |

The first two are queued as separate tasks.

content.text: Last piece: the at-a-glance diagram. Loading the drawing guide.

# topic.diagram

## Diagram

Diagram = a widget node, shown where the doc's embed block points at it; the embed's `caption` = what the picture is of ("approval flow · 3 stages"). `C` = the doc
container. Its code = ONE module → `export default () => <svg viewBox='0 0 760 H' role='img' aria-label='<title words>'>…</svg>;` = a drawing with no data (flow, tree, map, pillars, 2x2) · a block body is fine: `export default () => { … return <svg …>…</svg>; };` with consts and lowercase helpers first · no clock, no random: the picture draws the same every time
call → make + place in ONE `batch` = TWO members: the widget `create`, then a prose `update` whose insert holds the embed (a drawing that no embed points at is never shown); the sentence of reading rides the SAME insert's `content`:
```
batch(container = C, batch = [
 {"$lid":"w","verb":"create","object":"node","engine":"widget",
  "payload":{"parent":{"object":"file","id":"<tab file id: minted in that file's ack, not the ack's id>"},
   "code":"export default () => <svg viewBox='0 0 760 120' role='img' aria-label='Only a green build reaches production' fontSize='13'><text data-claude-text-id='title' x='24' y='28' fontSize='15' fontWeight='600' fill='var(--cds-text-primary)'>Only a green build reaches production</text>…</svg>;"}},
 {"verb":"update","ref":{"object":"node","id":"<body id>"},"engine":"prose",
  "payload":{"ops":[{"op":"insert","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["<block id>"]},"side":"after",
   "source":{"as":"markdown","blocks":{"dia":{"type":"embed","ref":"node/$lid:w","caption":"release flow · 5 steps, 1 decision"}},
    "from":{"kind":"inline","content":"<?claude block dia?>\n\nA failed test run loops back to the author; only a green build reaches production."}}}]}}
])
```
At the doc's birth: widget member BEFORE the prose member, the `<?claude block dia?>` token inside the markdown.

- HOW MUCH IT CARRIES — two readers, and the ask tells you which: someone who asks HOW a system works, what lives where, who owns what or why a step exists wants each box to carry its explanation — a name and the few lines that answer them, a key when colour carries a kind; a picture of bare names sends that reader back to the prose to find out what each box is for · someone who asks for the flow at a glance, the order of steps or where one thing sits wants few words and reads the shape · both are good drawings: a dozen explained boxes inside their containers is as right for the first reader as five bare boxes for the second · what limits a picture is the reader's glance and the column it sits in (where it lives, below), not a count: a picture that asks too much of one glance can become two, or keep its upper levels and hand the leaves to a table or to the sentence under it

labels → EVERY text element whose words you TYPE carries its OWN literal id, to the last one — title, names, body lines under a name, notes, edge labels, axis titles: `<text data-claude-text-id='<slug>' …>words</text>` · a typed text without an id cannot be edited or commented in place · words on a SCALE are printed from rows, not typed (`scale words`, below) · LITERAL id on LITERAL words = people edit the words in place + comment on that one label · written out one by one, outside loops: shapes may come from `.map()` or a helper, words may not — `nodes.map(n => <text data-claude-text-id={n.id}>{n.label}</text>)` → refused `text-id` + `text-literal` · a literal inside `.map()` = ONE label drawn many times · two lines = two `<tspan data-claude-text-id='…'>`, one id per line; an id on the `<text>` that holds tspans → refused `text-literal` · title = the first `<text>` · each id once per drawing
id → a short slug of the label's own words: letters, digits, _ and -, at most 64 · checkout · retries · step-legal · the same words after a redraw = the same id (edits and comments hang on it)
scale words → words that carry a POSITION (a date on a time line, a tick, a value that sets a length) are printed FROM the row that places their mark, not typed beside it: `<text {...datum(r,'date')}>{day(r.date)}</text>` at `X(r.date)` · why: ONE cell places the mark AND prints its words, so they cannot disagree — typed under a text id, a person edits "Oct 20" in place, the marker stays, and the drawing lies · to move it, change the cell: mark and words follow · a click on the printed date comments on that cell; Edit is not offered · id OR `datum`, never both: an id on computed words → refused `text-literal` · ticks = computed from the scale's steps, inside the axis's named group; the last one = `ticks.at(-1)`, never `ticks[ticks.length - 1]` (a computed index stages `eval-family`) · the names beside the marks stay typed under ids, each placed by its row's key, so a re-sorted row keeps its name (ex.4)
groups → ONE `<g data-claude-anchor='<slug>'>` per box / lane / pillar around its shape + its labels = people comment on that part by name · the name = a string literal, or in a loop a template ``{`lane-${i}`}``; a bare variable `{n}` → refused `segment-literal`
helpers → a lowercase function called in braces, `{box(cx, cy, 'b1')}` · a component → ONLY at the top of the module (`const Box = (…) => …` before `export default`); `<Box>` declared inside a function → refused `unknown-component` · a position by key → a literal read `pos.commit`, never `pos[k]`
data → numbers, dates, anything placed on a scale (a time line, Gantt bars, axis ticks, bar lengths) come from rows → a `claude.Visualize data-claude-component='<slug>'` with `sources={{rows:{kind:'data', data:[{…}, …]}}}` + `({rows, datum})` + `{...datum(row,'col')}` on every mark AND printed value that draws a row, as `topic.charts` spells it · spread the `datum(…)` call itself: a choice between two, or a result held in a const → refused `provenance` · without the component slug a click on a stamped mark does nothing, silently · pass the row you were GIVEN and derive values inline (`r.usd / total`, `day(r.date)`), never build new row objects (the copy stamps nothing, silently)
three ways to address what you draw:
| what | carries | people can |
|---|---|---|
| words YOU write (names, titles, notes) | `data-claude-text-id='<constant id>'` on its own `<text>` | edit in place + comment |
| text or marks drawn from rows (a milestone + its date words) | `{...datum(row, '<column>')}` on the mark and the `<text>` | comment (to change it, change the row: mark and words follow) |
| a part that is not words (the connectors, a zone, an axis) | `data-claude-anchor='<slug>'` on its `<g>` | comment |
traps (the validator reads the module; each of these stages it with errors) → a computed index — `xs[i]`, `pos[k]` → `xs.at(i)`, a literal read `pos.commit` · `top`, `parent`, `self`, `window` are the browser's names for its window objects (a way out of the widget), so the door refuses them as identifiers, locals too — a top edge is `y0`: `const cx = 290, y0 = 84`; a top row, `rowA`
LITERAL OR REFUSED → text ids, label words, group names = typed out in the JSX, never computed: `nodes.map(n => … {n.id} … {n.label} …)` stages with errors (`text-id`, `text-literal`; `data-claude-anchor={n}` → `segment-literal`) · loop boxes and lines, then write every `<text>` by hand, positions by literal read (`pos.commit.x`)
change → people edit a drawing's labels in place + comment on its parts: their words + their comments' anchors live in the module (label words, text ids, group names) · a smaller change leaves more of that byte for byte + the door records the change itself (what was quoted, what replaced it) · three roads, best = the smallest that does the job · words on a label → the text arm by id, no basePub → `update( ref = {"object":"node","id":"<widget id>"}, engine = "widget", container = C, payload = {"kind":"text","id":"step-legal","value":"Counsel sign-off"} )` · a small code change (a colour, a number, one shape) → `read` the widget, then `payload = {"kind":"draft-edit","edits":[{"quote":{"exact":"rowB = 230"},"replacement":"rowB = 238"}]}`: `exact` = stored code copied as read, matching exactly ONCE (`prefix` / `suffix` = the text right before / after it, when it matches more) · `"replacement":""` = delete it → ack `report.status` `"staged"` = STAGED ONLY, the page has NOT changed → THEN `payload = {"kind":"publish"}` → ack `outcome` `"published"` · a staged edit never published = a change nobody sees (ex.3) · anything bigger (several shapes, a new layout, a label added or gone) → redraw: the WHOLE module again, best written from the last `read` — label words as read (people edit them; retyped from memory = their edits undone) + text ids kept (comments hang on them) → `payload = {"kind":"draft","basePub":<pub>,"code":"export default () => …"}`
draft-edit refused (nothing changed) → `quote-not-found`: your quote is not in the stored code — `read` the widget again, copy the exact stored text (`value.draft.code` when a draft is open, else `value.code`) · `quote-ambiguous`: it matches more than once → add `prefix` / `suffix`, or a longer `exact` · up to 64 edits a call, applied in order, all or none · `draft-edit` is never refused for invalid code: it stages it and its ack says so (`report.status` `"staged-with-errors"` + the diagnostics) · the validator refuses at `publish`: `widget-invalid`, the detail names the rule and line:col; the page keeps the last publish, the draft stays staged → fix it with another `draft-edit`, or redraw
look → a screenshot read shows the render you write without seeing — `read( ref = {"object":"node","id":"<widget id>"}, engine = "widget", container = C, payload = {"kind":"screenshot"} )`, its own call (as a batch member it is refused `batch-shape`), always through `read`: `update` has no `screenshot` kind and refuses it `shape` → a PNG of the drawing as the page draws it in the light theme: the staged draft when one is open, else what is published · in it you can see a line running over its border, words cut at the frame's edge, an arrow through a name, how dense it reads at a glance · a `draft-edit` stages without publishing, so a correction can be looked at before `publish` puts it on the page (change → above; ex.3) · it may be worth checking quality this way; how, when and whether is your call · refused `unavailable` → its `detail` says when a retry helps; `data.problem` `"dark"` = no renderer here, a retry will not change it
where it lives → the drawing sits in a doc's text column, prose and tables above and below it, in front of someone scrolling: they take the picture in at a glance, react to its density before reading a word, and read the small words only if the glance pays · that column is 672 px wide in a laptop window, and the svg is scaled to fill it whatever its viewBox: a 760 frame shows at 0.88 (an authored 13 lands at 11.5 px), a 1100 frame at 0.61 (the same 13 lands at 8 px, under what people read), and on a phone the 760 frame shows at about 0.45 · height is free: the page scrolls and nothing is shrunk to fit a height, so a picture that needs room grows DOWN, not wide · what falls outside the viewBox is cut off, never shrunk into view
frame → viewBox='0 0 760 H' · H = the drawing's own height + a margin of about 24, the drawing centred, no empty band (in code a top edge is `y0` — traps) · every label inside it, ≥ 24 clear on the right · role='img' aria-label='<title words>'
screen reader → role='img' makes it treat the drawing as ONE image and skip the labels inside · aria-label = the name it says; with none it says only "image" · the name = what the picture shows (the title's words are enough)
title → the first `<text>` says what the picture shows, the finding a reader should leave with ("Only a green build reaches production"), not its topic ("Deployment process"): the point lands before the boxes are read, and the same words name the drawing for a screen reader (above) · a highlight that neither the title, a note nor a key explains reads as decoration
type size → fontSize at least 10.5 · what must be read: 13 · a 760 frame shows at about 0.88 of its size in a document, so an authored 10 lands under 9 px
the look · norms, depart when the picture earns it → colour is read as meaning: a reader asks what each colour stands for · emphasis works by contrast: one strong box among quiet ones is found at once, five are not · same kind of box = same fill · text 15 / 13 / 11.5, names fontWeight='600' · corners rx='8' · borders and connectors strokeWidth 1 to 1.25 · a coloured line takes its own marker in that colour (a marker does not take the line's colour) · steps of 8, ≥ 16 between boxes · labels textAnchor='middle', y = centre + fontSize/3 · shadows and gradients read as slideware beside a doc's flat type
arrowheads → ONE `<marker id='<slug>-arrow' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--cds-chart-axis)'/></marker>` in `<defs>` + `markerEnd='url(#<slug>-arrow)'` ON each connector · JSX names: `markerEnd` `strokeWidth` `textAnchor` `fontSize` `fontWeight` `fillOpacity`
colour → tokens only, light + dark for free (no hex, no named colour) · every `<text>` sets `fill` (no fill = black, unreadable on the dark page): words `var(--cds-text-primary)`, quiet words `var(--cds-text-secondary)` · borders, connectors, arrowheads `var(--cds-chart-axis)` · quiet rules `var(--cds-chart-grid)` · box fill 'none' · a tinted band `var(--cds-chart-reference-tint)` · an accent = `var(--cds-chart-categorical-1)`: `strokeWidth='2'` + the same token as fill at `fillOpacity='0.12'`, words on it stay text-primary · a stated meaning → `var(--cds-chart-status-good)`, `-warning`, `-critical` · more hues → `categorical-2…8` · `<style>`, `<use>` and `<foreignObject>` are refused ("not an element widgets may render"): presentation attributes, a helper or `.map()` for what repeats, a second `<tspan>` for a second line
connectors → in the gaps between boxes, never across a box or over a label · start and end ON a box edge · a far target → an elbow around the boxes between, not a line through them
loose parts → a box, a bar or a note with no tie to the rest reads as an afterthought, and the reader cannot tell what it belongs to · what is in the picture is tied to the thing it acts on: by a line, by sitting inside its container, or by sharing its axis
edge labels → beside their line with a clear gap (above a level run, right of an upright one), never on it · gap between two boxes narrower than the label → the label goes above the row
box width → svg does not wrap: YOU break every line, and a line that is too long runs over its border or is cut at the frame's edge · a box = its longest line of words + 24 · a 15/600 name runs about 8.5 units a character, a 13/600 name 7.4, a 13 line 7, an 11.5 line 6.2 → a line holds about (width − 24) / units characters (a 226 box: 27 of a 13/600 name, 32 of an 11.5 line · a 340 box: 50 of an 11.5 line) · at a 16 line height a box of a name + n body lines is 40 + 16 n tall (the name's baseline 24 down, the first body line's at 40, each next one 16 lower), and a badge row under the name adds 28 (the lines then start at 68) · a container = 32 for its name line, its children 16 in from its sides and 16 above its foot · you write without seeing the render, so count each line against its box before you send · too long → widen the box or break the line in two, never words on the border
words in the picture → only what the ask or the doc states · no invented numbers, durations, percentages, paths, parts or loops · detail unknown → leave it out
already in the doc → keep it: a redraw keeps every text id on its words · an existing ```mermaid block → edit it in place, never convert it · an existing chart → it stays a chart, changed as `topic.charts` says (A LATER CHANGE)
deck layouts · the geometry that makes each read (rows + a list hide it: the fall, the order, the spacing in time):
a placed item = a claim → place only what the ask or the doc states · unknown → its zone, no finer position
2x2 → two named axes, low → high · four named quadrants · items = labelled dots
stakeholder map → a 2x2: power up, interest right
pillars → roof = the goal · columns, initiatives inside · a base of enablers
driver tree → left to right from the result · the operator (× + −) between siblings
issue tree → left to right from the question
funnel → stages stacked, each as wide as its count against the first stage's (a ratio from the rows: the fall IS the picture, and even steps hide a fivefold drop) · count + name beside any bar too thin to hold them, the share that carries on between · its counts are data → a `claude.Visualize` with the stage counts as `sources` (`stages:{kind:'data', data:[{stage:'Visited', count:12000}, …]}`) + `{...datum(row,'count')}` on every stage, as `topic.charts` spells it; stage names = literal `<text>` with ids · magnitudes to compare → a chart
flywheel → nodes on a ring, one direction · the reinforcing link named
market map → segments = named zones · players = chips inside
value chain → chevrons left to right · support activities = bands under them
roadmap → phases = bands left to right along time, each with its name, its dates, its one line · gates = named diamonds on a phase edge, the gate's criteria = a short label under it · equal bands, not to scale → a plain module, dates typed · placed BY date → `timeline`
timeline → a time axis TO SCALE, ticks at even steps (weeks, months) · a row per item (or a lane per team), its typed name at the left · a span = a bar from start to end, a milestone = a diamond on its date, the date words beside the mark — all from `sources` rows (`scale words`) · a date = an ISO string in its row (`'2026-10-20'`): `Date.parse` places it, its words are cut from the string (a local-time getter such as `getDate()` prints the day before west of Greenwich) · the month word = a fixed list read with `.at(m - 1)`, never `months[m - 1]`: the door stages a computed index as `eval-family`, `.at()` is the accepted spelling · the ONE date that matters = the accent + a dashed line down the rows (ex.4)
date words and the dashed line → that line crosses every row, and date words in its path read as struck out · they sit on their mark's far side, or the line stops short of their row
before / after → two small flows, same scale · the change marked with the accent
operating model → layers top down · who decides what, named in each

# topic.diagram

## Diagram

Diagram = a widget node, shown where the doc's embed block points at it; the embed's `caption` = what the picture is of ("approval flow · 3 stages"). `C` = the doc
container. Its code = ONE module → `export default () => <svg viewBox='0 0 760 H' role='img' aria-label='<title words>'>…</svg>;` = a drawing with no data (flow, tree, map, pillars, 2x2) · a block body is fine: `export default () => { … return <svg …>…</svg>; };` with consts and lowercase helpers first · no clock, no random: the picture draws the same every time
call → make + place in ONE `batch` = TWO members: the widget `create`, then a prose `update` whose insert holds the embed (a drawing that no embed points at is never shown); the sentence of reading rides the SAME insert's `content`:
```
batch(container = C, batch = [
 {"$lid":"w","verb":"create","object":"node","engine":"widget",
  "payload":{"parent":{"object":"file","id":"<tab file id: minted in that file's ack, not the ack's id>"},
   "code":"export default () => <svg viewBox='0 0 760 120' role='img' aria-label='Only a green build reaches production' fontSize='13'><text data-claude-text-id='title' x='24' y='28' fontSize='15' fontWeight='600' fill='var(--cds-text-primary)'>Only a green build reaches production</text>…</svg>;"}},
 {"verb":"update","ref":{"object":"node","id":"<body id>"},"engine":"prose",
  "payload":{"ops":[{"op":"insert","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["<block id>"]},"side":"after",
   "source":{"as":"markdown","blocks":{"dia":{"type":"embed","ref":"node/$lid:w","caption":"release flow · 5 steps, 1 decision"}},
    "from":{"kind":"inline","content":"<?claude block dia?>\n\nA failed test run loops back to the author; only a green build reaches production."}}}]}}
])
```
At the doc's birth: widget member BEFORE the prose member, the `<?claude block dia?>` token inside the markdown.

- HOW MUCH IT CARRIES — two readers, and the ask tells you which: someone who asks HOW a system works, what lives where, who owns what or why a step exists wants each box to carry its explanation — a name and the few lines that answer them, a key when colour carries a kind; a picture of bare names sends that reader back to the prose to find out what each box is for · someone who asks for the flow at a glance, the order of steps or where one thing sits wants few words and reads the shape · both are good drawings: a dozen explained boxes inside their containers is as right for the first reader as five bare boxes for the second · what limits a picture is the reader's glance and the column it sits in (where it lives, below), not a count: a picture that asks too much of one glance can become two, or keep its upper levels and hand the leaves to a table or to the sentence under it

labels → EVERY text element whose words you TYPE carries its OWN literal id, to the last one — title, names, body lines under a name, notes, edge labels, axis titles: `<text data-claude-text-id='<slug>' …>words</text>` · a typed text without an id cannot be edited or commented in place · words on a SCALE are printed from rows, not typed (`scale words`, below) · LITERAL id on LITERAL words = people edit the words in place + comment on that one label · written out one by one, outside loops: shapes may come from `.map()` or a helper, words may not — `nodes.map(n => <text data-claude-text-id={n.id}>{n.label}</text>)` → refused `text-id` + `text-literal` · a literal inside `.map()` = ONE label drawn many times · two lines = two `<tspan data-claude-text-id='…'>`, one id per line; an id on the `<text>` that holds tspans → refused `text-literal` · title = the first `<text>` · each id once per drawing
id → a short slug of the label's own words: letters, digits, _ and -, at most 64 · checkout · retries · step-legal · the same words after a redraw = the same id (edits and comments hang on it)
scale words → words that carry a POSITION (a date on a time line, a tick, a value that sets a length) are printed FROM the row that places their mark, not typed beside it: `<text {...datum(r,'date')}>{day(r.date)}</text>` at `X(r.date)` · why: ONE cell places the mark AND prints its words, so they cannot disagree — typed under a text id, a person edits "Oct 20" in place, the marker stays, and the drawing lies · to move it, change the cell: mark and words follow · a click on the printed date comments on that cell; Edit is not offered · id OR `datum`, never both: an id on computed words → refused `text-literal` · ticks = computed from the scale's steps, inside the axis's named group; the last one = `ticks.at(-1)`, never `ticks[ticks.length - 1]` (a computed index stages `eval-family`) · the names beside the marks stay typed under ids, each placed by its row's key, so a re-sorted row keeps its name (ex.4)
groups → ONE `<g data-claude-anchor='<slug>'>` per box / lane / pillar around its shape + its labels = people comment on that part by name · the name = a string literal, or in a loop a template ``{`lane-${i}`}``; a bare variable `{n}` → refused `segment-literal`
helpers → a lowercase function called in braces, `{box(cx, cy, 'b1')}` · a component → ONLY at the top of the module (`const Box = (…) => …` before `export default`); `<Box>` declared inside a function → refused `unknown-component` · a position by key → a literal read `pos.commit`, never `pos[k]`
data → numbers, dates, anything placed on a scale (a time line, Gantt bars, axis ticks, bar lengths) come from rows → a `claude.Visualize data-claude-component='<slug>'` with `sources={{rows:{kind:'data', data:[{…}, …]}}}` + `({rows, datum})` + `{...datum(row,'col')}` on every mark AND printed value that draws a row, as `topic.charts` spells it · spread the `datum(…)` call itself: a choice between two, or a result held in a const → refused `provenance` · without the component slug a click on a stamped mark does nothing, silently · pass the row you were GIVEN and derive values inline (`r.usd / total`, `day(r.date)`), never build new row objects (the copy stamps nothing, silently)
three ways to address what you draw:
| what | carries | people can |
|---|---|---|
| words YOU write (names, titles, notes) | `data-claude-text-id='<constant id>'` on its own `<text>` | edit in place + comment |
| text or marks drawn from rows (a milestone + its date words) | `{...datum(row, '<column>')}` on the mark and the `<text>` | comment (to change it, change the row: mark and words follow) |
| a part that is not words (the connectors, a zone, an axis) | `data-claude-anchor='<slug>'` on its `<g>` | comment |
traps (the validator reads the module; each of these stages it with errors) → a computed index — `xs[i]`, `pos[k]` → `xs.at(i)`, a literal read `pos.commit` · `top`, `parent`, `self`, `window` are the browser's names for its window objects (a way out of the widget), so the door refuses them as identifiers, locals too — a top edge is `y0`: `const cx = 290, y0 = 84`; a top row, `rowA`
LITERAL OR REFUSED → text ids, label words, group names = typed out in the JSX, never computed: `nodes.map(n => … {n.id} … {n.label} …)` stages with errors (`text-id`, `text-literal`; `data-claude-anchor={n}` → `segment-literal`) · loop boxes and lines, then write every `<text>` by hand, positions by literal read (`pos.commit.x`)
change → people edit a drawing's labels in place + comment on its parts: their words + their comments' anchors live in the module (label words, text ids, group names) · a smaller change leaves more of that byte for byte + the door records the change itself (what was quoted, what replaced it) · three roads, best = the smallest that does the job · words on a label → the text arm by id, no basePub → `update( ref = {"object":"node","id":"<widget id>"}, engine = "widget", container = C, payload = {"kind":"text","id":"step-legal","value":"Counsel sign-off"} )` · a small code change (a colour, a number, one shape) → `read` the widget, then `payload = {"kind":"draft-edit","edits":[{"quote":{"exact":"rowB = 230"},"replacement":"rowB = 238"}]}`: `exact` = stored code copied as read, matching exactly ONCE (`prefix` / `suffix` = the text right before / after it, when it matches more) · `"replacement":""` = delete it → ack `report.status` `"staged"` = STAGED ONLY, the page has NOT changed → THEN `payload = {"kind":"publish"}` → ack `outcome` `"published"` · a staged edit never published = a change nobody sees (ex.3) · anything bigger (several shapes, a new layout, a label added or gone) → redraw: the WHOLE module again, best written from the last `read` — label words as read (people edit them; retyped from memory = their edits undone) + text ids kept (comments hang on them) → `payload = {"kind":"draft","basePub":<pub>,"code":"export default () => …"}`
draft-edit refused (nothing changed) → `quote-not-found`: your quote is not in the stored code — `read` the widget again, copy the exact stored text (`value.draft.code` when a draft is open, else `value.code`) · `quote-ambiguous`: it matches more than once → add `prefix` / `suffix`, or a longer `exact` · up to 64 edits a call, applied in order, all or none · `draft-edit` is never refused for invalid code: it stages it and its ack says so (`report.status` `"staged-with-errors"` + the diagnostics) · the validator refuses at `publish`: `widget-invalid`, the detail names the rule and line:col; the page keeps the last publish, the draft stays staged → fix it with another `draft-edit`, or redraw
look → a screenshot read shows the render you write without seeing — `read( ref = {"object":"node","id":"<widget id>"}, engine = "widget", container = C, payload = {"kind":"screenshot"} )`, its own call (as a batch member it is refused `batch-shape`), always through `read`: `update` has no `screenshot` kind and refuses it `shape` → a PNG of the drawing as the page draws it in the light theme: the staged draft when one is open, else what is published · in it you can see a line running over its border, words cut at the frame's edge, an arrow through a name, how dense it reads at a glance · a `draft-edit` stages without publishing, so a correction can be looked at before `publish` puts it on the page (change → above; ex.3) · it may be worth checking quality this way; how, when and whether is your call · refused `unavailable` → its `detail` says when a retry helps; `data.problem` `"dark"` = no renderer here, a retry will not change it
where it lives → the drawing sits in a doc's text column, prose and tables above and below it, in front of someone scrolling: they take the picture in at a glance, react to its density before reading a word, and read the small words only if the glance pays · that column is 672 px wide in a laptop window, and the svg is scaled to fill it whatever its viewBox: a 760 frame shows at 0.88 (an authored 13 lands at 11.5 px), a 1100 frame at 0.61 (the same 13 lands at 8 px, under what people read), and on a phone the 760 frame shows at about 0.45 · height is free: the page scrolls and nothing is shrunk to fit a height, so a picture that needs room grows DOWN, not wide · what falls outside the viewBox is cut off, never shrunk into view
frame → viewBox='0 0 760 H' · H = the drawing's own height + a margin of about 24, the drawing centred, no empty band (in code a top edge is `y0` — traps) · every label inside it, ≥ 24 clear on the right · role='img' aria-label='<title words>'
screen reader → role='img' makes it treat the drawing as ONE image and skip the labels inside · aria-label = the name it says; with none it says only "image" · the name = what the picture shows (the title's words are enough)
title → the first `<text>` says what the picture shows, the finding a reader should leave with ("Only a green build reaches production"), not its topic ("Deployment process"): the point lands before the boxes are read, and the same words name the drawing for a screen reader (above) · a highlight that neither the title, a note nor a key explains reads as decoration
type size → fontSize at least 10.5 · what must be read: 13 · a 760 frame shows at about 0.88 of its size in a document, so an authored 10 lands under 9 px
the look · norms, depart when the picture earns it → colour is read as meaning: a reader asks what each colour stands for · emphasis works by contrast: one strong box among quiet ones is found at once, five are not · same kind of box = same fill · text 15 / 13 / 11.5, names fontWeight='600' · corners rx='8' · borders and connectors strokeWidth 1 to 1.25 · a coloured line takes its own marker in that colour (a marker does not take the line's colour) · steps of 8, ≥ 16 between boxes · labels textAnchor='middle', y = centre + fontSize/3 · shadows and gradients read as slideware beside a doc's flat type
arrowheads → ONE `<marker id='<slug>-arrow' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--cds-chart-axis)'/></marker>` in `<defs>` + `markerEnd='url(#<slug>-arrow)'` ON each connector · JSX names: `markerEnd` `strokeWidth` `textAnchor` `fontSize` `fontWeight` `fillOpacity`
colour → tokens only, light + dark for free (no hex, no named colour) · every `<text>` sets `fill` (no fill = black, unreadable on the dark page): words `var(--cds-text-primary)`, quiet words `var(--cds-text-secondary)` · borders, connectors, arrowheads `var(--cds-chart-axis)` · quiet rules `var(--cds-chart-grid)` · box fill 'none' · a tinted band `var(--cds-chart-reference-tint)` · an accent = `var(--cds-chart-categorical-1)`: `strokeWidth='2'` + the same token as fill at `fillOpacity='0.12'`, words on it stay text-primary · a stated meaning → `var(--cds-chart-status-good)`, `-warning`, `-critical` · more hues → `categorical-2…8` · `<style>`, `<use>` and `<foreignObject>` are refused ("not an element widgets may render"): presentation attributes, a helper or `.map()` for what repeats, a second `<tspan>` for a second line
connectors → in the gaps between boxes, never across a box or over a label · start and end ON a box edge · a far target → an elbow around the boxes between, not a line through them
loose parts → a box, a bar or a note with no tie to the rest reads as an afterthought, and the reader cannot tell what it belongs to · what is in the picture is tied to the thing it acts on: by a line, by sitting inside its container, or by sharing its axis
edge labels → beside their line with a clear gap (above a level run, right of an upright one), never on it · gap between two boxes narrower than the label → the label goes above the row
box width → svg does not wrap: YOU break every line, and a line that is too long runs over its border or is cut at the frame's edge · a box = its longest line of words + 24 · a 15/600 name runs about 8.5 units a character, a 13/600 name 7.4, a 13 line 7, an 11.5 line 6.2 → a line holds about (width − 24) / units characters (a 226 box: 27 of a 13/600 name, 32 of an 11.5 line · a 340 box: 50 of an 11.5 line) · at a 16 line height a box of a name + n body lines is 40 + 16 n tall (the name's baseline 24 down, the first body line's at 40, each next one 16 lower), and a badge row under the name adds 28 (the lines then start at 68) · a container = 32 for its name line, its children 16 in from its sides and 16 above its foot · you write without seeing the render, so count each line against its box before you send · too long → widen the box or break the line in two, never words on the border
words in the picture → only what the ask or the doc states · no invented numbers, durations, percentages, paths, parts or loops · detail unknown → leave it out
already in the doc → keep it: a redraw keeps every text id on its words · an existing ```mermaid block → edit it in place, never convert it · an existing chart → it stays a chart, changed as `topic.charts` says (A LATER CHANGE)

content.text:
It's a function call. The popup text is the message, and the thing every warning goes through is one helper function. My sentence mixed the two up, and it also overstated the coverage.

**What the code does.** While Orca loads a 3MF, it works out which program made the file and which version. Several branches of that check can warn the user. Each branch calls the same small helper, `log_and_show_3mf_info(text, title)`, passing its message text ([Plater.cpp:6063](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:6063)). The helper writes the text to the log, then calls `show_info`, which opens the popup. That one call is where the hook would go.

**The correction.** Not every 3MF message goes through that helper. Seven do: the version and "made in another program" messages. The "Modified G-code" and "Customized Preset" warnings open their own popups directly, so covering them needs two more small hooks.

I've fixed this in the report. The "One catch point in Orca" step now says it's a helper function that each check calls, and names the two warnings that go around it. I also changed the diagram's box to read "each version check calls one popup helper".

content.content:
1:# JusPrin production architecture
2:
3:**Status:** Selected architecture and production implementation boundary for `jusprin-newui`.
4:
5:JusPrin replaces OrcaSlicer's primary presentation and workflow, while retaining OrcaSlicer's mature manufacturing behavior. Product work must simplify how users express intent and verify a print; it must not fork slicing, geometry, rendering, picking, serialization, or history behavior.
6:
7:## Product composition
8:
9:The target project window has four stable regions:
10:
11:1. A compact machine and project status row.
12:2. A collapsible, thin plates and objects pane.
13:3. OrcaSlicer's existing Prepare or G-code Preview canvas.
14:4. A fixed Agent conversation and print-plan pane.
15:
16:The compact plates/objects pane is deferred to a later task. The first
17:production shell and Agent implementation must not depend on it; users interact
18:with objects through the native canvas and Agent until the pane is added.
19:
20:Prepare is the persistent workspace. **Check print** temporarily replaces its center canvas with Orca's real sliced Preview. **Print** opens Send preflight and never sends immediately. Project details are a drawer, and Monitor is a separate surface that can remain visible during other work.
21:
22:## Runtime architecture
23:
24:```text
25:OrcaSlicer process (C++17 / wxWidgets / OpenGL)
26:├── JusPrin application shell
27:│   ├── compact top navigation and machine status
28:│   ├── native plates/objects pane
29:│   ├── center workspace host
30:│   │   ├── existing GLCanvas3D Prepare canvas
31:│   │   └── existing G-code Preview canvas
32:│   └── wxWebView
33:│       └── local React/TypeScript Agent interface
34:├── typed workspace/controller boundary
35:├── existing Orca model, selection, plates, gizmos, and undo stack
36:└── existing slicing, project I/O, device, and print subsystems
37:```
38:
39:The boundary is deliberately conservative:
40:
41:- The viewport and overlays over the viewport remain native.
42:- The top row and object/plate pane start as native wxWidgets.
43:- C++ owns application and project state.
44:- The WebView receives versioned events and sends versioned commands.
45:- A WebView object pane may be evaluated later only as a contained presentation choice. It does not justify Electron or a WebGL viewport.
46:
47:## Authoritative ownership
48:
49:| Concern | Authoritative owner | JusPrin responsibility |
50:|---|---|---|
51:| Project model and object identity | Orca `Model` and `ObjectID` | Project a typed, session-scoped view |
52:| Plates and active plate | Orca `PartPlateList` | Present and request changes through commands |
53:| Selection and picking | Orca `Selection` and `GLCanvas3D` | Synchronize UI without feedback loops |
54:| Geometry transforms | Orca gizmos and `GizmoObjectManipulation` | Launch existing behavior and present exact values |
55:| Undo and redo | Orca undo stack | Expose availability and outcomes without a shadow stack |
56:| Slicing and Preview | Orca slicing actions and Preview canvas | Present Slice and Check print states |
57:| Project serialization | Orca 3MF and model serializers | Preserve compatibility; add migration only for new data |
58:| Agent conversation | React/TypeScript WebView | Render messages, write the words people and the model read, and submit typed commands (see [Where logic goes](#where-logic-goes-the-page-first)) |
59:| Agent print plan | C++/agent application boundary | Explain intent, decisions, uncertainty, and consequences |
60:
61:## Production integration boundaries
62:
63:### Shell host
64:
65:Use one fork-owned shell installed through one small `MainFrame` attachment. Startup policy belongs to a fork-owned bootstrap or shell factory, not to a growing collection of environment checks inside Orca constructors.
66:
67:The first production version may keep the legacy top bar, tab panel, Sidebar, and `GUI_ObjectList` constructed when existing Orca behavior depends on them. They should be excluded from the visible layout, not covered by a separate top-level window. Removing their construction is a separate lifecycle project.
68:
69:### Build registration
70:
71:Keep the explicit JusPrin source list in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/sources.cmake`. Orca's central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt` should contain one stable include rather than a growing list of fork-owned files.
72:
73:### Workspace boundary
74:
75:The production workspace API should retain the useful POC concepts: strong plate and object IDs, read-only snapshots, explicit command errors, typed change reasons, monotonic revisions, and move-only RAII subscriptions. Before production use it must also:
76:
77:- define GUI-thread requirements;
78:- define exactly when a revision advances;
79:- invalidate session IDs explicitly when a project is replaced;
80:- observe changes made outside the adapter;
81:- report history independently of widget visibility;
82:- report whether undo and redo actually changed authoritative state;
83:- avoid depending on `GUI_ObjectList` for model commands;
84:- provide plate selection, object import/addition, and other product-required commands;
85:- remain free of wxWidgets and Orca types in its public contract.
86:
87:When an operation is trapped in presentation code, expose the smallest behavior-oriented command from its current owner. Do not copy the operation into JusPrin and do not simulate input against hidden controls.
88:
89:### Canvas presentation
90:
91:Retain a product-neutral presentation API on `GLCanvas3D` and a fork-owned RAII controller that applies JusPrin policy and restores previous Orca state. Visibility and input must be independently controllable so invisible chrome cannot consume pointer events while active native gizmos remain usable.
92:
93:Production controls should be more granular than the POC's broad `render_overlays` switch. Independently classify the stock main toolbar, gizmo picker, active gizmo handles, plate actions, object labels, layer-editing controls, navigation aids, Preview legend, and Preview sliders. Shared controls such as Plater's collapse toolbar need one owner at the shell lifetime, not one guard per canvas.
94:
95:### Plates and objects pane (deferred)
96:
97:This pane remains part of the target product, but it is not part of the current
98:production-shell or Agent-WebView task and is not a prerequisite for either.
99:When it is scheduled, the production pane is intentionally smaller than
100:`GUI_ObjectList`.
101:
102:It must:
103:
104:- list and switch plates;
105:- list objects on the active plate;
106:- synchronize selection in both directions;
107:- add/import, rename, duplicate, and remove an object;
108:- expose less common operations through a selected-object menu, More, or the Agent;
109:- expand into a full tree only for multi-object, multi-part, multi-material, modifier, or print-order complexity.
110:
111:Every command must reuse Orca's snapshot, cancellation, plate-membership, selection, update, and serialization behavior.
112:
113:### Agent WebView
114:
115:The production Agent interface is a standalone local React/TypeScript package embedded in `wxWebView`. It requires:
116:
117:- a versioned command/event schema;
118:- deterministic mock conversations for UI tests;
119:- incremental message rendering and stable scroll anchoring;
120:- explicit keyboard, focus, shortcut, clipboard, selection, and IME rules;
121:- reload, startup, bridge-error, and unavailable-agent states;
122:- no direct ownership of Orca project state.
123:
124:#### Where logic goes: the page first
125:
126:When the same logic could live either in C++ or in a React page, put it in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++. The page is quicker to change (Vite hot reload instead of relinking a multi-gigabyte GUI library), its tests run in milliseconds under Vitest, and it is already where the words people read are written. The words the model reads belong there too.
127:
128:Strong reasons for C++:
129:
130:- **It reads or changes OrcaSlicer state:** presets, the model, plates, slicing, the device list. The page never owns project state (see the constraints below).
131:- **It is a limit or a boundary the app must guarantee:** what a tool accepts and refuses, which tools a session may call, what needs the person's approval, and what reaches the model provider (API keys, access codes, project data). Page code can state a limit; only the app can enforce it.
132:- **It has to work without a page:** the MCP server, background work, tests that run without a browser.
133:- **It depends on a thread or a lifetime the page does not have.**
134:
135:The printer panel is the example. The app sends the page facts only: sizes, spools, which printer is on a card, what a change changed. The page writes every word from them. It writes the model's instructions (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`) and hands them over with `printer_instructions`. It writes the panel's own words, the opening line and the note that goes with each tap (`AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts`). The opening goes over with `printer_opening`, and a tap's note travels in the tap's payload.
136:
137:The app decides the tools -- the five printer tools and the four settings tools, the same in every mode -- checks every call, refuses one that does not fit the conversation (adding a printer outside an Add conversation, changing a printer other than the one it is about, a setting of anything but that printer), and refuses a turn that has no instructions rather than falling back to the project assistant's prompt. It posts the opening once per session, and a tap's note only when the tap goes through, bounded to 2 KB. It still writes the notes for what only it can find out when the tap arrives: the network printer has gone, its model id is not on the list, or a save or undo failed.
138:
139:Windows uses WebView2, macOS uses WKWebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK. Local resource packaging must work on all three. The demonstrated prototype used a single-file local bundle to avoid WKWebView `file:` subresource failures; production keeps that approach, and CMake now produces the bundle from the TypeScript/React sources.
140:
141:MCP and broad agent autonomy are later layers. They must use the same typed boundary rather than changing viewport ownership.
142:
143:### Gizmo presentation
144:
145:Start with Move or Rotate and create one reusable native controller seam around existing behavior:
146:
147:1. Show a compact action strip in the Prepare canvas's upper-left corner: a horizontal row, the way OrcaSlicer's own toolbar runs, but justified left rather than centred. It does not follow the selection or the camera: a strip docked to the object jumps whenever the view orbits. `Canvas/ViewportToolStrip` draws it with ImGui inside the canvas's own frame, through `GLCanvas3D::set_overlay_renderer`, and reads the open tool from the gizmo manager every frame. The open tool's values hang below the row in `Canvas/ToolValuePanel`, aligned with the button that opened it.
148:2. Activate the existing native gizmo.
149:3. Preserve existing pointer manipulation, snapping, and selection.
150:4. Route exact numeric entry through `GizmoObjectManipulation`.
151:5. Preserve existing snapshot timing and undo/redo.
152:6. Dismiss without inventing a draft transaction; Undo remains the revert path unless product requirements explicitly change.
153:
154:Then convert tools by interaction family: Move/Rotate/Scale; Mirror/Duplicate/Place on face; Measure; Cut/Repair; Text/Emboss; painter-based tools.
155:
156:### Semantic annotations
157:
158:Reuse existing painter raycasting, brush selection, clipping, facet visualization, copying, undo, and 3MF persistence. The unproven production delta is arbitrary semantic labels and their agent-facing representation. The first implementation should use two labels on one object and verify save/reload, transforms, duplication, undo/redo, and behavior under topology changes before expanding the palette.
159:
160:## Non-negotiable constraints
161:
162:- Do not change slicing algorithms for UI convenience.
163:- Do not replace `GLCanvas3D` or G-code Preview.
164:- Do not reimplement geometry operations in TypeScript.
165:- Do not place WebView content over the native GL canvas.
166:- Do not create a JavaScript shadow project model or undo stack.
167:- Preserve 3MF projects, printer profiles, shortcuts, serialization, and cross-platform behavior.
168:- Do not seek stock Orca feature parity when the product definition does not require it.
169:- Do not reopen Electron or WebGL without a new explicit product decision backed by evidence.
170:
171:## Implementation order
172:
173:1. Establish canonical product documents, design tokens, and curated assets.
174:2. Productionize the workspace contract, canonical Orca commands, observation, and real-adapter tests.
175:3. Productionize the canvas presentation/controller seam.
176:4. Build the production shell without a compact object/plate pane.
177:5. Build the typed Agent WebView and bridge.
178:6. Add the Move/Rotate presentation controller and roll out gizmo families.
179:7. Add semantic annotations, Check print reporting, Send preflight, Monitor, calibration, and troubleshooting surfaces according to the product definition.
180:8. Add the compact object/plate pane as a separately planned task when it is prioritized.
181:
182:Historical implementations and detailed proof are intentionally not copied here. See [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

99:When it is scheduled, the production pane is intentionally smaller than
100:`GUI_ObjectList`.
101:
102:It must:
103:
104:- list and switch plates;
105:- list objects on the active plate;
106:- synchronize selection in both directions;
107:- add/import, rename, duplicate, and remove an object;
108:- expose less common operations through a selected-object menu, More, or the Agent;
109:- expand into a full tree only for multi-object, multi-part, multi-material, modifier, or print-order complexity.
110:
111:Every command must reuse Orca's snapshot, cancellation, plate-membership, selection, update, and serialization behavior.
112:
113:### Agent WebView
114:
115:The production Agent interface is a standalone local React/TypeScript package embedded in `wxWebView`. It requires:
116:
117:- a versioned command/event schema;
118:- deterministic mock conversations for UI tests;
119:- incremental message rendering and stable scroll anchoring;
120:- explicit keyboard, focus, shortcut, clipboard, selection, and IME rules;
121:- reload, startup, bridge-error, and unavailable-agent states;
122:- no direct ownership of Orca project state.
123:
124:#### Where logic goes: the page first
125:
126:When the same logic could live either in C++ or in a React page, put it in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++. The page is quicker to change (Vite hot reload instead of relinking a multi-gigabyte GUI library), its tests run in milliseconds under Vitest, and it is already where the words people read are written. The words the model reads belong there too.
127:
128:Strong reasons for C++:
129:
130:- **It reads or changes OrcaSlicer state:** presets, the model, plates, slicing, the device list. The page never owns project state (see the constraints below).
131:- **It is a limit or a boundary the app must guarantee:** what a tool accepts and refuses, which tools a session may call, what needs the person's approval, and what reaches the model provider (API keys, access codes, project data). Page code can state a limit; only the app can enforce it.
132:- **It has to work without a page:** the MCP server, background work, tests that run without a browser.
133:- **It depends on a thread or a lifetime the page does not have.**
134:
135:The printer panel is the example. The app sends the page facts only: sizes, spools, which printer is on a card, what a change changed. The page writes every word from them. It writes the model's instructions (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`) and hands them over with `printer_instructions`. It writes the panel's own words, the opening line and the note that goes with each tap (`AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts`). The opening goes over with `printer_opening`, and a tap's note travels in the tap's payload.
136:
137:The app decides the tools -- the five printer tools and the four settings tools, the same in every mode -- checks every call, refuses one that does not fit the conversation (adding a printer outside an Add conversation, changing a printer other than the one it is about, a setting of anything but that printer), and refuses a turn that has no instructions rather than falling back to the project assistant's prompt. It posts the opening once per session, and a tap's note only when the tap goes through, bounded to 2 KB. It still writes the notes for what only it can find out when the tap arrives: the network printer has gone, its model id is not on the list, or a save or undo failed.
138:
139:Windows uses WebView2, macOS uses WKWebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK. Local resource packaging must work on all three. The demonstrated prototype used a single-file local bundle to avoid WKWebView `file:` subresource failures; production keeps that approach, and CMake now produces the bundle from the TypeScript/React sources.
140:
141:MCP and broad agent autonomy are later layers. They must use the same typed boundary rather than changing viewport ownership.
142:
143:### Gizmo presentation
144:
145:Start with Move or Rotate and create one reusable native controller seam around existing behavior:
146:
147:1. Show a compact action strip in the Prepare canvas's upper-left corner: a horizontal row, the way OrcaSlicer's own toolbar runs, but justified left rather than centred. It does not follow the selection or the camera: a strip docked to the object jumps whenever the view orbits. `Canvas/ViewportToolStrip` draws it with ImGui inside the canvas's own frame, through `GLCanvas3D::set_overlay_renderer`, and reads the open tool from the gizmo manager every frame. The open tool's values hang below the row in `Canvas/ToolValuePanel`, aligned with the button that opened it.
148:2. Activate the existing native gizmo.
149:3. Preserve existing pointer manipulation, snapping, and selection.
150:4. Route exact numeric entry through `GizmoObjectManipulation`.
151:5. Preserve existing snapshot timing and undo/redo.
152:6. Dismiss without inventing a draft transaction; Undo remains the revert path unless product requirements explicitly change.
153:
154:Then convert tools by interaction family: Move/Rotate/Scale; Mirror/Duplicate/Place on face; Measure; Cut/Repair; Text/Emboss; painter-based tools.
155:
156:### Semantic annotations
157:
158:Reuse existing painter raycasting, brush selection, clipping, facet visualization, copying, undo, and 3MF persistence. The unproven production delta is arbitrary semantic labels and their agent-facing representation. The first implementation should use two labels on one object and verify save/reload, transforms, duplication, undo/redo, and behavior under topology changes before expanding the palette.
159:
160:## Non-negotiable constraints
161:
162:- Do not change slicing algorithms for UI convenience.
163:- Do not replace `GLCanvas3D` or G-code Preview.
164:- Do not reimplement geometry operations in TypeScript.
165:- Do not place WebView content over the native GL canvas.
166:- Do not create a JavaScript shadow project model or undo stack.
167:- Preserve 3MF projects, printer profiles, shortcuts, serialization, and cross-platform behavior.
168:- Do not seek stock Orca feature parity when the product definition does not require it.
169:- Do not reopen Electron or WebGL without a new explicit product decision backed by evidence.
170:
171:## Implementation order
172:
173:1. Establish canonical product documents, design tokens, and curated assets.
174:2. Productionize the workspace contract, canonical Orca commands, observation, and real-adapter tests.
175:3. Productionize the canvas presentation/controller seam.
176:4. Build the production shell without a compact object/plate pane.
177:5. Build the typed Agent WebView and bridge.
178:6. Add the Move/Rotate presentation controller and roll out gizmo families.
179:7. Add semantic annotations, Check print reporting, Send preflight, Monitor, calibration, and troubleshooting surfaces according to the product definition.
180:8. Add the compact object/plate pane as a separately planned task when it is prioritized.
181:
182:Historical implementations and detailed proof are intentionally not copied here. See [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

1032:## Definition of done
| `settings_preview_patch` | Check a batch before requesting approval | read-only | both | required `scope`: process, one object, or a filament or printer preset by name | `IWorkspace::preview_settings` using a clone and scope-specific validation/normalization | at most 32 input keys; bounded changes, dependencies, issues and warnings |
| `settings_search` | Find a setting without loading the full catalog | read-only | both | required `scope`: process, one object, or a filament or printer preset by name | `IWorkspace::search_settings` using Orca definitions filtered by scope | 1–25 matches; deterministic cursor paging and bounded metadata |
| `slice_inspect` | Look inside a slice: layers or G-code | read-only | both | one plate's current slice | `GCodeProcessorResult::moves` and the plate's G-code file | 100 layers per page (index, z, height, time, 16 roles, speed, fan, temperature and flow ranges) or 64 KB of G-code, with `next` |
| `slice_report` | Check a sliced plate before committing to it | read-only | both | one plate's current slice | `Print` statistics and the plate's `GCodeProcessorResult`; `BuildVolume` for the bed check | 16 filaments, 32 findings, critical first; Orca's send-dialog advisories only as Orca shows them (`appliesWhen: timelapse`, the bed-temperature one never); 32 support contacts, seam regions, first-layer objects and islands; intent checks |
| `slice_start` | Slice without leaving the conversation | mutation (computation-only; `preempt` restores the card) | both | one plate, or every plate | `Plater`'s own toolbar slice events | handle plus the slicing section |
| `view_render` | See the plate | read-only | both | one plate, prepare mode | `GLCanvas3D::render_thumbnail` with the 3MF thumbnail's parameters | one PNG, 64 to 1280 px a side, beside its size and mime type |
| `workspace_inspect` | Client needs current project context | read-only | both | current document | `IWorkspace::snapshot`, plus `IProductState` for intent and plan | at most 16 plates, 64 objects across returned plates and 64 selected IDs; labels at most 256 UTF-8 bytes; totals and truncation flags; `activities` lists the latest 20 tool calls with state, plan and error |

`workspace_inspect` takes an optional `sections` list — `summary` (the default, and exactly what it returned before sections existed), `project`, `objects`, `intent`, `plan`, `slicing`, `printer`. The `objects` section lists every object (64, then `truncated`) with its plates, instance/part/modifier counts, printable flag, extruder, size and override count, from a separate adapter call so the snapshot every selection change builds stays cheap; it has no cursor yet. The `slicing` section also carries `jobs`: each Orca UI job a tool started (orient, arrange), with its handle, state, and for arrange the objects no plate holds afterwards. The `project` section reports the file's path, saved and preset-edit state, the file's own title, designer, description, license, copyright and origin (each `{value, provenance: "project_file"}`, present only when the file states it), the packed attachments by id (a read-only walk of the auxiliary folder without `JusPrin/` and `.thumbnails`; `ProjectPanel::Reload` would create folders), and whether an automatic backup covers the latest edits. The `printer` section sets the configured side (preset, model id, nozzles, plate, filament materials) beside the selected machine, with the facts the person confirmed under `factKey` (`device:<id>` when a machine is selected, otherwise `preset:<name>`) and computed `mismatches` for model, nozzle, filament material, and plate. No printer Orca talks to reports its plate, so `plateObservable` is false and a plate mismatch can only come from a confirmed fact. Its output schema requires only the identity fields, so a caller that asks for one section is not handed the rest. It is no longer a strict OpenAI function: strict mode cannot express an optional argument.

Intent and plan writes do not advance the workspace revision, and that is deliberate — see [JusPrin-owned project state](#jusprin-owned-project-state). The intent vocabulary is the agent's own; an entry carrying a question and no value is what it asked and does not know, which is where `openQuestions` comes from.

`printer_setup_preview` never selects anything. It evaluates a candidate against the free `is_compatible_with_printer`, with the same `printer_preset`/`num_extruders` extra config `update_compatible_internal` builds, and reads the plates a printer offers from its vendor model's `not_support_bed_types`, as the sidebar does. Which preset Orca substitutes for one that stops fitting is its own scoring, so the preview names what will be replaced, not what replaces it; `printer_setup` reads the outcome back and reports it. Orca's `Tab::select_preset` asks about unsaved edits in a modal, so the setup counts them first (every edited preset when the printer changes, otherwise the one being switched), refuses with `unsaved_edits`, and only with `unsavedEdits: "discard"` drops them through `discard_current_changes` before selecting. There is no "keep" yet: carrying edits across a switch is Orca's transfer path, not implemented here. The proposal stores the previewed outcome as `confirmedSetup`, and execution refuses with `stale_workspace` if a fresh preview differs. `confirmFacts` go to the app-data facts store under the printer section's `factKey`, each with its own lifetime.

Verified against the in-process fake Bambu printer (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md`): printer_list and the printer section show FAKE001 idle, then printing at 40% with temperatures and job from the control file; a preview of an uninstalled 0.2 nozzle preset and of an unoffered plate is refused without a revision change; an approved setup of plate, process and filament read back the new selection and, with a confirmed "Cool Plate (SuperTack)", a `user_confirmed` plate mismatch; a process switch with one unsaved edit was refused, then applied with `discard`, and no dialog window was open afterwards.

`project_open` takes exactly one of `path` and `new: true`. Orca asks its load-path questions in modals scattered through `Plater::priv::load_files`, `load_model_objects` and `close_with_confirm`; every one of them opens through `DPIAware::ShowModal`, so the fork adds a two-line hook there that asks the innermost `ScopedModalAnswers` (`JusPrin/Workspace/ModalAnswers.cpp`) for the answer. The adapter answers "Object too small" from `unitConversion`, "Object too large" from `oversized`, and Orca's save prompt with No only when the caller passed `unsavedWork: "discard"`; any other message dialog gets No and any other dialog Cancel, the choices that change least, and every question and answer is returned in `decisions`. Edited presets are discarded before the load, so `UnsavedChangesDialog`, whose answer is read from the dialog afterwards, never asks. A `.3mf` opens with its settings through Orca's own `"<silence>"` origin; `loadProjectSettings: "keep"` sets the geometry-only load behaviour for that one load, which is the answer the person would give in `ProjectDropDialog`. A model file becomes a new project named after it, with `ImperialUnits` for `unitConversion: "inches"`. The adapter does not rely on the load's own return for projects; it compares the project file afterwards.

Replacing the project tears down the old project's tool state (`AgentHost::on_document_replaced`), which ran while `project_open` itself was still executing. The coordinator now keeps the executing activity through `clear()`, the `project_open` branch finds its record again by id after the load, and `McpRuntime::detach_calls` leaves that one call attached, so an MCP client gets its result. In-app, opening a project ends the chat it was asked from, because that conversation belongs to the project being closed.

`object_analyze` handles are `f<revision>-<object>-<part>-<plane>-<feature>`: the Measure module numbers planes deterministically from the lowest facet, so the same revision finds the same feature again, and any other revision fails with `feature_expired`. Features come from one `Measuring` per model part on its untransformed mesh, moved to the world with the first instance's matrix, as the measure gizmo builds them; face area is summed from the plane's triangles because the module never fills it, and a plane whose border cannot be walked is dropped. A hole is a circular border that its own face does not cover (a boss's rim is covered); the module has no cylinder detection, so a hole is reported by its mouths. Unit suspicion asks Orca's own load-time tests of a model holding only a copy of the object. `orientations` asks the new `orientation::score_orientations` seam for the costs `orient()` ranks by (`unprintability`, weighted overhang, bed contact), for given up directions or face handles, or for Orca's own candidates, on the instance's rotated parts with `OrientJob`'s parameters; the catalog's "support volume" is not something Orca computes, so it is not reported.

`object_place` applies units, scale, mirror, then one of face-down, rotation or auto-orient, then position and drop, inside one `Plater::TakeSnapshot`, through the same `Selection` calls and `GLCanvas3D::do_*` commits the gizmos use (face-down passes the flatten gizmo's snapshot name so a sinking object stays on the bed). `unitsFix` goes through `Plater::convert_unit`, which replaces the object, so the result names the new id. Two catalog facets changed against the real owner: `autoOrientFor` is `autoOrient`, because Orca's auto-orient optimises only for minimal support — the other goals are served by scoring candidates with `object_analyze` and placing the chosen face down — and `arrangeAfter` is left to `plate_layout`. Auto-orient runs `OrientJob` under a `ReportingJob` wrapper that reports finished, cancelled (including dropped from the queue) or failed into the slicing section's jobs.

Verified against the app with Orca's bundled Voron cube: 3,414 facets, round holes of 13–16 mm with their axes, a side face put down (the old handle then refused as expired), rotate/scale/mirror/drop and scale-to-size, auto-orient finishing as a job, one "Place object" undo step per call, and a 20 mm cube written in metres flagged as `meters` and converted to 20 mm under a new object id.

`plate_layout` checks every row before anything moves, then applies plates (a row without an id adds one through the add-plate path, less its own snapshot), then objects: printable through the object list's own toggle steps, quantity through Orca's `increase_instances`/`decrease_instances` on the selected object (which refuse a disabled or cut object, and never with a count that would remove the object), a plate move as a relative move by the difference of plate origins, the name through the fork's `rename_object`, and the extruder as an object override. All of that is one "Lay out plates" undo step. Arrange sets the canvas spacing and rotation for the run and restores them when the job ends; with a plate id it arranges that plate (Orca's menu state), otherwise every unlocked plate. Orca does not report what did not fit (its `m_unarranged` is never filled), so the job's `notPlaced` is every printable instance no plate holds entirely afterwards. Two catalog details changed against the owner: `sequence` is not offered (print order is a per-plate setting and belongs with the settings tools), and arrange has no "selected" scope (`ArrangeJob` never calls its `prepare_selected`).

**M3 eval, 2026-09-16, Windows, fake Bambu A1 mini.** Over MCP (the scripted client in place of Claude Code, approvals through the page's decision hook): a 1 × 0.5 × 0.25 block written in inches was imported (Orca asked "Object too small", answered no), `object_analyze` reported `unitsSuspicion: inches`, `unitsFix` made it 25.4 × 12.7 × 6.35 mm under a new id, the 25.4 × 6.35 face was put down by handle, quantity 2 and arrange all finished with nothing unplaced, and `fit` put both copies inside the plate with the 161.29 mm² face on the bed — pass. In-app with OpenAI and the file attached to the chat, five runs, reviewed per the handoff:

- Run 1 exposed a page bug, not a model one: the test hook's `send` kept the first render's staged-attachment list and never sent the file, so the model had no import tool, invented a path for `project_open`, and was refused. Fixed in `App.tsx` (the send reads the current state).

The adapter does not rely on the load's own return for projects; it compares the project file afterwards.

Replacing the project tears down the old project's tool state (`AgentHost::on_document_replaced`), which ran while `project_open` itself was still executing. The coordinator now keeps the executing activity through `clear()`, the `project_open` branch finds its record again by id after the load, and `McpRuntime::detach_calls` leaves that one call attached, so an MCP client gets its result. In-app, opening a project ends the chat it was asked from, because that conversation belongs to the project being closed.

`object_analyze` handles are `f<revision>-<object>-<part>-<plane>-<feature>`: the Measure module numbers planes deterministically from the lowest facet, so the same revision finds the same feature again, and any other revision fails with `feature_expired`. Features come from one `Measuring` per model part on its untransformed mesh, moved to the world with the first instance's matrix, as the measure gizmo builds them; face area is summed from the plane's triangles because the module never fills it, and a plane whose border cannot be walked is dropped. A hole is a circular border that its own face does not cover (a boss's rim is covered); the module has no cylinder detection, so a hole is reported by its mouths. Unit suspicion asks Orca's own load-time tests of a model holding only a copy of the object. `orientations` asks the new `orientation::score_orientations` seam for the costs `orient()` ranks by (`unprintability`, weighted overhang, bed contact), for given up directions or face handles, or for Orca's own candidates, on the instance's rotated parts with `OrientJob`'s parameters; the catalog's "support volume" is not something Orca computes, so it is not reported.

`object_place` applies units, scale, mirror, then one of face-down, rotation or auto-orient, then position and drop, inside one `Plater::TakeSnapshot`, through the same `Selection` calls and `GLCanvas3D::do_*` commits the gizmos use (face-down passes the flatten gizmo's snapshot name so a sinking object stays on the bed). `unitsFix` goes through `Plater::convert_unit`, which replaces the object, so the result names the new id. Two catalog facets changed against the real owner: `autoOrientFor` is `autoOrient`, because Orca's auto-orient optimises only for minimal support — the other goals are served by scoring candidates with `object_analyze` and placing the chosen face down — and `arrangeAfter` is left to `plate_layout`. Auto-orient runs `OrientJob` under a `ReportingJob` wrapper that reports finished, cancelled (including dropped from the queue) or failed into the slicing section's jobs.

Verified against the app with Orca's bundled Voron cube: 3,414 facets, round holes of 13–16 mm with their axes, a side face put down (the old handle then refused as expired), rotate/scale/mirror/drop and scale-to-size, auto-orient finishing as a job, one "Place object" undo step per call, and a 20 mm cube written in metres flagged as `meters` and converted to 20 mm under a new object id.

`plate_layout` checks every row before anything moves, then applies plates (a row without an id adds one through the add-plate path, less its own snapshot), then objects: printable through the object list's own toggle steps, quantity through Orca's `increase_instances`/`decrease_instances` on the selected object (which refuse a disabled or cut object, and never with a count that would remove the object), a plate move as a relative move by the difference of plate origins, the name through the fork's `rename_object`, and the extruder as an object override. All of that is one "Lay out plates" undo step. Arrange sets the canvas spacing and rotation for the run and restores them when the job ends; with a plate id it arranges that plate (Orca's menu state), otherwise every unlocked plate. Orca does not report what did not fit (its `m_unarranged` is never filled), so the job's `notPlaced` is every printable instance no plate holds entirely afterwards. Two catalog details changed against the owner: `sequence` is not offered (print order is a per-plate setting and belongs with the settings tools), and arrange has no "selected" scope (`ArrangeJob` never calls its `prepare_selected`).

**M3 eval, 2026-09-16, Windows, fake Bambu A1 mini.** Over MCP (the scripted client in place of Claude Code, approvals through the page's decision hook): a 1 × 0.5 × 0.25 block written in inches was imported (Orca asked "Object too small", answered no), `object_analyze` reported `unitsSuspicion: inches`, `unitsFix` made it 25.4 × 12.7 × 6.35 mm under a new id, the 25.4 × 6.35 face was put down by handle, quantity 2 and arrange all finished with nothing unplaced, and `fit` put both copies inside the plate with the 161.29 mm² face on the bed — pass. In-app with OpenAI and the file attached to the chat, five runs, reviewed per the handoff:

- Run 1 exposed a page bug, not a model one: the test hook's `send` kept the first render's staged-attachment list and never sent the file, so the model had no import tool, invented a path for `project_open`, and was refused. Fixed in `App.tsx` (the send reads the current state).
